chunks: "The noisy nodes of a buck are the switch node, the hot loop, and the inductor with its stray field.
The switch node swings the full input voltage in a few nanoseconds, so any copper area on it couples through capacitance.
The hot loop, input capacitor plus both switches, carries pulses of the load current with nanosecond edges, so it makes a magnetic field and voltage spikes.
The inductor has a magnetic field, and the bootstrap and gate-drive loops are smaller versions of the same thing.
Then there's the pulsed current on the input line, which is conducted noise.
For routing: keep each of these as short and small as possible, on one layer, with no vias, and with a solid ground plane right beneath so the fields terminate there rather than somewhere else.
The switch node should be just wide enough for the inductor current, no pours, no test pad bigger than needed.
Keep sensitive nets, like feedback, away from it and don't route anything underneath or alongside it.

Other board-level things: put the converter in its own corner of the board, away from analog, RF and crystals; use a shielded inductor; filter the input with a small LC or a ferrite so noise doesn't leave on the supply line; keep the supply's connectors and cables away from the noisy nodes because cables make great antennas; and if needed add a snubber across the low-side switch to damp the ring."
